extracted.intended_audience: sellers offering negative-option features, company compliance officers, legal counsel, and stakeholders responding to FTC rulemaking
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory standards implementing the FTC's final Rule on negative-option features (disclosures, misrepresentations, cancellation, and related compliance obligations). Intended to inform businesses and counsel how to comply with §425 provisions and related statutory/precedential limits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materiality standard for misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission applies its established materiality standard, limiting enforcement to misrepresentations that are likely to affect consumers' choice of, or conduct regarding, goods or services.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites In re Cliffdale Assocs., Inc., 103 F.T.C. 110 (1984) and related authorities; in the negative-option context the Commission alleges misrepresentations intended to induce consumers to enter negative option programs. Commenters asked for more specificity; Commission refers to Policy Statement on Deception and related TSR provisions for discussion of reasonableness and materiality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to disclose all material terms (§425.4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Sellers are required to disclose all material terms of the transaction (changed in final Rule from 'any' to 'all'), not limited to terms related solely to the negative option feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This aligns with ROSCA requirements; the Commission deleted the phrase 'related to the underlying good or service that is necessary to prevent deception' for clarity. The disclosures provision uses 'and including' to make listed disclosures always material rather than merely examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific required disclosure: amount (or range) and frequency of charges
rubrics_metrics.description: The final Rule requires sellers to disclose 'The amount (or range of costs) the consumer will be Charged and, if applicable, the frequency of the Charges a consumer will incur unless the consumer takes timely steps to prevent or stop those Charges.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission retained this specific disclosure as always material. Commenters suggested additional specificity about deadlines, amounts, or ranges; Commission expects sellers to include cost information (including recurring costs and total costs) to avoid deception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of material cost misrepresentations
rubrics_metrics.description: In the negative-option context, material cost misrepresentations may include any cost (and total costs) from inception through the course of the commercial relationship, including misrepresentations as to recurring costs and refunds or guarantees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supported by numerous enforcement cases (listed) showing costs, recurring charges, refunds, and guarantees are presumptively material; examples and case citations provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclosure clarity standard — 'diction and syntax' understandable to ordinary consumers
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosures must 'use diction and syntax understandable to ordinary consumers.' The Commission declined to replace that phrasing with 'words and grammar.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission emphasized that 'diction and syntax' is clearer, especially for audio disclosures. Commenters (e.g., NFIB) proposed alternate wording, but Commission retained original phrasing for clarity across media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misrepresentations provision examples vs. mandatory disclosures construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The misrepresentations provision (§425.3) uses 'including' to provide examples of potentially material facts, while the disclosures provision uses 'and including' to signal that listed disclosures are always material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinction affects whether a listed item is merely illustrative (misrepresentations provision) or a required, always-material disclosure (disclosures provision).

rubrics_metrics.name: Simple cancellation mechanism requirement (§425.6)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Rule requires sellers to provide a simple cancellation mechanism for negative option features.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Commission expects this, together with disclosure and misrepresentation prohibitions, to address concerns about providing consumers 'all the information necessary' to cancel; the reminders requirement will further address retention of important information. Commenters asked for clarity on how cancellation information must be provided and made findable; IAB suggested concise disclosures of where cancellation information is located.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on retaining/using consumer payment information without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a violation of Section 5 for a seller to retain and use a consumer's payment information without the consumer's consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: FTC enforcement cases cited (e.g., Classic Closeouts LLC). The Commission cited Amazon v. FTC (ROSCA context) clarifying that consumers must be given the choice to autofill or provide billing information only after receiving disclosures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing of billing/authorization relative to disclosures (ROSCA timing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Consumers must be given the choice to autofill billing information or otherwise provide payment information after the required disclosures; disclosures must precede collection/use of payment authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites FTC v. Amazon.com and ROSCA: companies may offer autofill but consumers must be given the choice after disclosures. Compliance with the Rule does not guarantee compliance with Regulation E/EFTA authorization requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: EFTA / Regulation E carve-out and non-conflict consideration
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed provision does not apply to transactions covered by the preauthorized transfer provision of EFTA (15 U.S.C. 1693e) and Regulation E (12 CFR 1005.10) to avoid conflict with those statutes/regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulation E contains prescriptive requirements (e.g., written consumer signatures under E-Sign, evidence of identity, inclusion of terms in authorization, provision of a copy) that go beyond measures in the Rule, so compliance with the Rule alone may not assure Reg E compliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: B2B negotiated-terms exemption (as applied in Vonage order)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Vonage order exempted negative option feature provisions in B2B contracts where defendants possess evidence that consumers negotiated significant terms of the negative option feature that are only negotiable with business consumers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The final Rule is described as less prescriptive and more flexible than that court order, promoting more marketplace flexibility. The Commission discusses B2B contexts and whether/when negative-option provisions should be treated differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'save' (efforts to retain consumers) and its permissible scope
rubrics_metrics.description: The proposed Rule defined 'save' as an attempt by a seller to present additional offers, modifications, or reasons to retain the existing offer when a consumer attempts to cancel a negative option feature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many commenters argued the definition is overly broad and would prohibit useful, consumer-friendly clarifications; industry groups asked to allow short clarification/confirmation follow-ups or immediate discussion of pause/skip/modification options without prior permission.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement, prominence, and accessibility of online/mobile disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters raised practical concerns about requirements that online or mobile disclosures be 'unavoidable' and 'immediately adjacent,' especially on small screens.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments urged the Commission to hew to its .com Disclosures policy for consistency; concerns include how to implement 'unavoidable' and 'immediately adjacent' on constrained mobile UI and suggestions for making cancellation information easy to find and retain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reasonableness / puffery boundary
rubrics_metrics.description: Exaggerated advertising, boasting, or puffery on which no reasonable buyer would rely may be un-actionable and therefore outside the scope of actionable misrepresentations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commission declines to add a separate 'reasonable person standard' phrase but refers to the Policy Statement on Deception for discussion of reasonableness. Cites Direct Marketing Concepts and other cases distinguishing puffery from actionable claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reminders requirement to aid consumer retention of important information
rubrics_metrics.description: The Commission expects to address consumers' ability to retain important disclosure information through development of reminder requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State AGs asked for disclosures capable of being retained by consumers; the Commission expects the reminders requirement (and other Rule provisions) to encourage sellers to make information easy to find and retain while the Rule is implemented.
